editorial_title_zh: 奥利维耶·梅茨格：迎着夜色而行
editorial_excerpt_zh: 有些摄影师用光照亮万物。奥利维耶·梅茨格则寻找光线所隐匿之物，在酒店房门后、海绿色窗帘后、蒂尔达·斯文顿身着橄榄色西装的身影中寻觅它们。法国人常说“既来之，则安之”（à la guerre comme à la guerre）。梅茨格作出了同等的回应：他迎着夜色而行，任由琥珀色、钠灯光芒交织，沉浸在电影的迷离氛围中。

Some photographers light things up. Olivier Metzger looks for what light conceals, and finds it behind a hotel door, a sea-green curtain, the silhouette of Tilda Swinton in an olive suit. Take war as it comes, the French say, “à la guerre comme à la guerre.” Metzger answers in kind: he takes the night as it comes, amber, sodium-lit, haunted by cinema.

Born in Mulhouse in 1973, he first worked as a nurse. Caregiver, then director. At 28 he entered the École nationale supérieure de la photographie (ENSP) in Arles, graduated in 2004 and won the Prix Voies Off at the Rencontres the same year with his series “Data.” Then came Libération , Télérama , Le Monde , The New York Times (assignments, that genre where the subject sets the rules, and the hour too). Metzger slipped a dramaturgy into them, sculpting his images in “a delicate chiaroscuro, often tinged with melancholy.”

David Lynch surfaces quickly in critics’ pieces, and for good reason: in 2012, the filmmaker made the series “Smile (Forever)” his favorite at Paris Photo. A film? A dream? A hotel room? The doubt is maintained, and so is the fiction. Even a doe spotted by chance on a Nevada road ( Bambi, Nevada , 2010) enters it like a fairy tale. The world seems about to come apart, and Metzger lights it so that it holds a moment longer. Publisher Actes Sud introduces him as a “photographer of the strange.”

Then came the loss. On November 2, 2022, Olivier Metzger died in a road accident near Arles, his adopted city. In 2023, the Rencontres asked Éric Reinhardt for a tribute. The writer built his text from 49 songs drawn from the photographer’s Spotify library. 49 songs, 49 years. Three years later, the exhibition extends the echo, and the book, published in June 2026 (128 pages), takes the form of a two-voice dialogue fed by the music that accompanied Metzger. One can read it “as a farewell.” Reinhardt, the friend, wants us to feel an artist working “as if he were photographing his own destiny.” Even on assignment.

“Olivier Metzger, Somewhere and Somehow,” is on view at La Croisière , in Arles Arles, through October 4, 2026. The book Somewhere and Somehow is published by Actes Sud and available for €35.

article_text:
Anyone who saw Sandra Wollner’s perversely creepy previous film , “The Trouble with Being Born,” might be left having no idea what to expect from her follow-up. That film was built around a child-sized android cast in resemblance to her master’s missing daughter — and it’s more than implied he’s sexually assaulting the girl, too.

Disturbing as it was, “The Trouble with Being Born” also announced Wollner’s aptitude for capturing grief from peculiar, underseen angles. And so her next movie, “ Everytime ,” while more generously empathetic, also takes on loss from a mind-bending perspective we’re not going to spoil. Since winning in Cannes’ Un Certain Regard, this German entry for the Best International Feature Film Oscar has bewitched festivalgoers from Toronto to New York. IndieWire shares the exclusive teaser below.

“Everytime” also just received Gotham Award nominations for Best International Feature, Best Director, and Best Original Screenplay. Here, following a tragedy in Berlin, a mother, Ella (Birgit Minichmayr), her youngest daughter, Melli (Lotte Shirin Keiling), and her older daughter’s former boyfriend, Lux (Tristán López), take what turns out to be a profound holiday to the Spanish island of Tenerife — one where the environment appears to convene and reshape itself around their shared, unimaginable loss.

“Everytime” will play for a one-week Oscar-qualifying run at New York City’s Lincoln Center starting November 6, with the full theatrical date following February 12, 2027. 1-2 Special distributes the film after purchasing “Everytime” out of Cannes. The New York-based distributor also has Marine Atlan’s Cannes-winning “ La Gradiva ,” entering theaters in December.

“Its ineffable power belongs to how matter-of-factly Wollner tears apart the fabric of her film’s reality at the same time as she threads it together,” Indiewire’s David Ehrlich wrote of “Everytime” in his Grade A review.

Watch the teaser for “Everytime” below.

Films and events

Love

Mouse

Katherine Mallen Kupferer and Sophie Okonedo excel in this moving drama about facing up to life in the aftermath of a tragedy.

Screening dates and booking

Check which tickets are still available across the festival – and find out about extra ticket releases and standby queues .

Credits

Directors Kelly O’Sullivan, Alex Thompson

Screenwriter Kelly O’Sullivan

With Katherine Mallen Kupferer, Sophie Okonedo, Chloe Coleman

USA 2026. 120min

Courtesy of Altitude

Language English

Introduction

Lifelong friends Callie and Minnie are like ying and yang: one loud and popular, the other shy and quiet. Abruptly forced out from her friend’s shadow, it’s finally time for Minnie to figure out who she is on her own terms. Kupferer and Okonedo’s performances drive this beautiful film that’s guaranteed to have audiences alternating between crying and laughing out loud.

Grace Barber-Plentie

How to book

Tickets start from £10 for all screenings and events in London, with concessions available for many screenings. Booking information and ticket prices .

For non-Members we charge £1 per ticket for online and phone bookings, up to £3 per transaction. There’s no booking fee if you buy tickets at the box office.

If you’re aged 16 to 25, sign up for free to BFI 25 and Under for a chance to get £6 tickets (without booking fees) to all screenings and events, subject to availability.

Missed out?

More tickets may become available for these screenings before and during the festival. Find out about extra ticket releases and standby queues .

Our programmers recommend...

7 Miles Out

Carol Morley (Dreams of a Life, The Falling) adapts her moving semi-autobiographical novel, capturing her adolescence in Stockport during the 70s and 80s.

Hot Water

This atmospheric and sharply funny road movie sees a Lebanese mother and her American son take a trip, with a lot to unpack along the way.

Josephine

Winner of the Grand Jury Dramatic Prize at Sundance, this suspenseful and devastating film follows a child trying to navigate life after witnessing a sexual assault.

Pocket Review

Ilana Savdie and Chaïm Soutine Shed the Skin

An exhibition pairing paintings by the two artists guides us through the chambers of our own minds and bodies.

Hyperallergic )

If Chaïm Soutine hangs up carcasses to dry, Ilana Savdie dissects them with surgical precision. Pairing the Jewish Belarusian and Colombian-American artists seems obvious: Soutine wrestled the turmoil of both World Wars onto canvas, and Savdie melts modern life's cacophony into oozing creatures of our own making. Coming face to face with their work, I felt a strange mix of alienation and recognition at once.

It’s odd to stand in a New York City gallery amid these chimeras of two eras roiling with violence and uncertainty. The rebellious, frenetic hand of Soutine , who moved to Paris two years before World War I began and went into hiding during the Nazi occupation in 1940, charged his early paintings on view here with static shocks that still have the power to jolt us. In “Hanging Turkey” (circa 1925), echoing his admiration of El Greco, Soutine transforms an unremarkable scene into a portrait of torture. The plucked turkey resembles a decapitated angel, its beak open as if in anguish even after death.

article_text:
On December 11, 2025, as part our annual winter list extravaganza, Film Comment Editors Devika Girish and Clinton Krute were joined by esteemed critics Amy Taubin and Bilge Ebiri for a real-time countdown of the films topping our year-end critics’ poll . The evening featured a lively discussion (and some hearty debate) about the films as they were unveiled—and now it’s here in Podcast form, for your home-listening pleasure. Consider it a holiday gift from us to you, our loyal listeners.

Read the full list, plus Best Undistributed Films, individual ballots, and more, here .

editorial_title_zh: 《鲸落》影评——黏稠的生存惊悚片将我们困在鲸鱼体内，却难以让人完全消化

article_text:
Spare a thought for poor Austin Abrams, who, having just endured the world’s worst, and gloopiest, courier assignment in Resident Evil , has now been trapped inside a sperm whale …

The immensely likable Euphoria alum (has any show in recent memory provided quite as many genuine stars?) brings what he can to Brian Duffield’s rather soggy adaptation of Pulitzer prize-winner Daniel Kraus’s acclaimed novel Whalefall. But there’s not a great deal he can do, despite being in every scene of what’s his second studio lead in a month, other than scream and writhe and look understandably alarmed. It’s a setup that’s grabby enough to have us wonder just how the hell it’s going to play out (what if that one scene in Finding Nemo but a whole movie) but it just doesn’t work as a 106-minute adventure, too overstretched and too silly to have us rooting for his escape and caring how he might orchestrate it.

There is something charmingly ambitious about a writer choosing to write himself into a corner, making an already hard job even harder, because while Kraus could clue readers into his protagonist’s inner thoughts and fears, Duffield decides against the easier choice of a voiceover. In order to keep the scenario as grounded as possible, Abrams’ unfortunate hero Jay is also unable to remove his breathing apparatus as the air inside the whale is toxic so whatever talking he might do is muffled through a mouthpiece. The authenticity is applaudable but it’s just one of many decisions that makes it harder to justify and enjoy the stage-to-screen adaptation, our connection to his plight hard to solidify.

We learn more about Jay via a series of flashbacks, fleshing out his relationship to a gruff and difficult father ( Josh Brolin ), who recently chose killing himself in the ocean rather than dying slowly of mesothelioma, a rare cancer. Jay is determined to find his body, for reasons never quite fully explained, and after he’s trapped inside a whale, he looks back on their fractured dynamic, usefully accompanied by nuggets of diving wisdom from his father. Jay has something to prove (his mostly awful-seeming dad tells him he has “soft lungs”) and so his journey out of the beast is one that also aims to show what he can do by himself.

Duffield’s scripts can often feel like pitches that are more sellable in an elevator than films that are watchable on the big screen, and while Whalefall might be his first adaptation, it suffers from the same disappointing follow-through. There was The Babysitter (what if your babysitter was a devil-worshipper), Spontaneous (what if spontaneous combustion at high school), No One Will Save You (what if home invasion but aliens) and the most relevant here, Underwater (what if monsters at the bottom of the ocean). As director, he does a better job than that film’s William Eubank did at capturing the majesty and terror of the water (he also only has one character to focus on and make distinguishable) but while treating the whale’s body as an alien landscape is an interesting idea, it’s also a limiting one.

Given this year’s deluge of shark movies , Whalefall makes an admirable initial case for finding drama elsewhere in the water. The otherworldly horror of the predicament is often wincingly effective (stomach acid burning hands, a swallowed-at-the-same-time giant squid causing added tentacled mayhem) and the film has a slick studio sheen that can be that much harder to find these days. But there are only so many set pieces that can take place in such a setting and only so much problem-solving that can be made legible without real dialogue. These scenes might get repetitive and viscerally unpleasant, yet they are at least more striking than the hopelessly rote and uninvolving father-son flashbacks that fail to add any real emotion or stakes to the story. What could have been a lean, mean 85-minute race to survive becomes weighed down by CW network-level soap, and Duffield never makes a decision we don’t already expect ( his influences for the film , a list that bizarrely includes Brokeback Mountain, A Little Prayer, JFK and West Side Story, fail to add any personality to the finished product). A final hallucinatory chat is also laughably ineffective as dead father asks potentially dying son the questions he always wanted to know (spoiler: they include “did you ever want a dog?”). Abrams is an actor who has become incredibly easy to root for, but he struggles to make his scenes with Brolin feel like anything other than treading water (I would have liked to see more of the forever underused Elisabeth Shue as his mother).

Flipping between a family drama of soul-searching and hackneyed advice-giving (“Survivors survive!”) and the more immediate 4DX-suited rush of thrashing, squelching, splashing and panicking makes Whalefall a disorienting and frustrating experience, like someone switching channels without your permission. You’ll want to grab the remote and watch something else entirely.

Whalefall is out in Australian cinemas on 15 October and in the US and UK on 16 October

Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s Situation-Chip is Meme Gold

The internet is having a field day after the tech mogul confessed to having an affair with a suspected Chinese intelligence spy.

After two Astronomer executives were caught canoodling on the jumbotron during a Coldplay concert last year, another tech CEO's extramarital affair has become the meme of the season. Since confessing to his affair with suspected Chinese spy Alice Huang on Sunday, November 8, Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang has set off a firestorm across the tech and geopolitical spheres and, to our amusement, social media.

In a message shared with his employees on November 8, the 63-year-old CEO acknowledged the affair and extended an apology to his wife, Lori Huang, and his two children, both of whom work for the chip-producing company valued at over $4 trillion. Jensen Huang is viewed as somewhat of a deity in the AI world, having founded Nvidia in a Denny’s restaurant booth in 1993 and turned it into a key player in the AI rivalry between China and the United States.

article_text:
W ith some of its showings in the huge Imax format, this National Geographic-backed documentary feels like a callback to the early, glory days of large-format cinema when it was all about spectacle and scale, turning footage of natural-world wonders into an immersive experience. Those with a fear of heights or prone to vertigo may find this all a bit too immersive, in fact. That’s even more the case considering the point of the movie appears to be to provoke anxiety in the viewer for nearly the entire running time as we watch the subjects scale the steeper, far less travelled north face of Mount Everest and then, for reasons never quite adequately explained, ski back down it again.

Such was the mission of experienced mountaineer Jim Morrison , an amiable-seeming fellow who, like all of those who pursue extreme sports, seems to feel a compulsion to put himself in the kind of grave danger that, should things go wrong, would put other people in danger rescuing him. His partner Hilaree Nelson shares his passion, and the two of them set off to be the first people to ski down Everest’s north face, and the first third of the film tracks them as they plan and eventually do practice runs to achieve this goal. Neither seems able to adequately explain why they’ve chosen to take such a risk, although Nelson tries a bit to articulate her mountaineering life almost as if it’s a career choice that her two teenage sons should simply accept as her choice to make, and maybe even thank her for – even if that means that should she be injured or lost they and Morrison (who is not the boys’ biological father) would also have to deal with the aftermath.

We don’t want to give away what happens, but these moral questions hang over this film in a much more obvious way than they do in most other mountain-climbing films. (Interestingly, this is also a work co-directed by another couple, Jimmy Chin and Elizabeth Chai Vasarhelyi, who appear on screen to thrash out their own feelings on risk and reward.) Meanwhile, there’s some thoughtful footage of the various Nepalese guides who assist in Jim and Hilaree’s adventures, local men who have been climbing these mountains all their lives because they have far fewer career choices than the western tourists who come through town with camera crews, swathed in brightly coloured, prominently logo-bearing sports equipment.

The lurid palette of this kit does in fact become a bit distracting when we get back to the mountain climbing stuff, and if you want to just relax and look at the stunning landscape you need to train your eyes to ignore the fluorescent jackets obstructing the view. That’s not criticising the cinematography itself; it is pin-sharp thanks to the most advanced kinds of lens and drone technology. But it’s safe to say the ethics aired here are a far murkier affair.

article_text:
The creator of the cult classic “ WNUF Halloween Special ” is back with another experimental seasonal project.

Writer-director Chris LaMartina has announced “ Spirit Tasting ,” a spooky New Year’s Eve-themed film from Terror Vision Original Productions.

Per the official synopsis, “A post-punk riff on ‘The Monkey’s Paw,’ Chris LaMartina’s ‘Spirit Tasting’ follows three former punks (Sean Doherty, Melissa LaMartina and Trevor Wilhelms) as they toast their late bandmate at a distillery on New Year’s Eve. When a strange sommelier (Matt Lake) invites them to a top-shelf tasting, they discover there’s only one catch: Every bottle requires a ‘wish.’ But as each of their desires twist into doom, these old friends discover that every pour at the Red Bat Distillery comes at a deadly price.”

Related Stories

Todd Haynes, Zhang Ziyi and Daniel Brühl Lead a Star-Studded Lumière Fest Opening With Haynes Teasing ‘De Noche,’ Starring Pedro Pascal

The film also stars Matt Baughman, Cate Paris and Tatiana Nya Ford, along with cameos from genre fixtures like Grady Hendrix, Clay McLeod Chapman, Peaches Christ and Henry Zebrowski. Chris LaMartina directed and edited the film, and co-wrote it with Michael Varrati. It is produced by Melissa LaMartina, Chris LaMartina, Varrati and Ted Geoghegan. It’s executive produced by Ryan Graveface.

Popular on Variety

In the spirit of B-movie icons like Roger Corman, the film was shot in four days for $40,000 in order to celebrate Chris LaMartina’s 40th birthday.

The film will also be screening in a holiday roadshow across the country with to-be-announced dates from November to early January. Chris LaMartina and select cast members will appear at each stop. A Blu-ray release will follow the roadshow.

Netflix has released a new set of images for The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth , the David Fincher film starring Brad Pitt and written by Quentin Tarantino.

Pitt reprises his role as Cliff Booth in the film, set for release November 25 in Imax and December 23 on Netflix.

The film also stars Elizabeth Debicki, Scott Caan, Carla Gugino, Yahya Abdul-Mateen II, Peter Weller, Matt Groove, JB Tadena, Corey Fogelmanis, Karren Karagulian.

RELATED: David Fincher Scrapped 60 Pages Of Tarantino’s ‘Cliff Booth’ Script: “It Was Essentially Two Movies”

Murder, blackmail, theft, extortion — just another summer in Hollywood. It’s 1977, eight years since Cliff Booth (Brad Pitt) encountered the Manson family in Tarantino’s parallel history of 1969, Once Upon a Time… in Hollywood .

The fairy tale is now over in The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth . Los Angeles no longer needs a hippie-slaying stuntman the way it did. But Hollywood will always have problems, problems that can only be solved by someone with Cliff’s unique (occasionally extralegal) abilities. When he’s not earning his keep bartending or as a projectionist, Cliff Booth is a fixer — solving situations for Hollywood’s great and, sometimes, not so good.

RELATED: ‘Wicker’ Red Carpet Premiere Photos: Olivia Colman, Alexander Skarsgård, Elizabeth Debicki & More

He’s curious when he gets a call from talent agent Karen Crosby (Debicki), on behalf of her client, TV megastar Charlie Peters (Scott Caan) — a man known for doing his own stunts. And he’s further entertained and intrigued when he meets other characters in Charlie’s world, from his knowing wife Toni (Gugino) to pro football champion turned screen star Roderick “Hot Rod” Harrison (Abdul-Mateen II). Then there are the Verdusco brothers (Groove and Tadena), mysterious gangsters causing mayhem across the city. What was once a fairytale is now a crime story — a cocktail of violence, ambition, and desire that could only happen in LA.
